extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students studying algebraic topology; readers learning cohomology, Bockstein homomorphisms, CW complexes, and limits/Ext
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and structural results for computing cohomology rings (including cup products) using CW structures, cellular homology, Bockstein homomorphisms, and limit/Ext methods; also methods for relating cohomology with Z and with field coefficients. Includes worked examples (Stiefel manifolds, lens spaces, RP^∞ products, SO(n)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced CW structure on Stiefel manifolds V_{n,k}
rubrics_metrics.description: View V_{n,k} as the coset space O(n)/O(n-k) (or SO(n)/SO(n-k) when appropriate). The projection O(n)→V_{n,k} (or SO(n)→V_{n,k}) is onto with fibers cosets αO(n-k); cells of V_{n,k} are cosets e_I SO(n-k) (with natural ordering) and form a CW structure with boundaries contained in lower-dimensional cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cellular map SO(n)→V_{n,k} to induce the cellular chain complex of V_{n,k} from that of SO(n). This gives explicit cellular boundary maps (e.g., V_{2k+1,2} reduces to previously defined C_{2k}, while for V_{2k,2} the boundary maps are trivial), enabling direct computation of homology of V_{n,k}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known homology of V_{n,2}
rubrics_metrics.description: For V_{2k+1,2}: H_i(V_{2k+1,2}; Z) = Z for i=0 and i=4k-1, and Z_2 for i=2k-1. For V_{2k,2}: H_i(V_{2k,2}; Z)=Z for i=0,2k-2,2k-1,4k-3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit homology groups follow from the cellular chain complexes induced from SO(n) and are used to compare SO(n) with products of V_{odd,2} factors (differences may appear in cup-product structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cup-product distinctions for SO(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although SO(n) can have the same homology groups as certain products of V_{*,2} (and possibly an extra sphere), SO(n) is often distinguished from these products by its cup product structure (e.g., β_1^4 nonzero in H^4(SO(n); Z_2) for n≥5 while corresponding product factors have H^4=0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume product decomposition from homology groups alone; compute cup products (possibly with Z_2 coefficients and Bocksteins) to detect nontrivial ring-level differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Bockstein homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a short exact sequence of coefficients 0→G→H→K→0, applying cohomology yields a long exact sequence; the boundary map H^n(X;K)→H^{n+1}(X;G) is the Bockstein homomorphism. In particular β: H^n(X; Z_m)→H^{n+1}(X; Z_m) associated to 0→Z_m→Z_{m^2}→Z_m→0 and related β: H^n(X;Z_m)→H^{n+1}(X;Z) associated to 0→Z→Z→Z_m→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Bockstein arising from coefficient short exact sequences to relate cohomology with Z coefficients to that with Z_m (especially m=p prime). The reduction map ρ: H^*(X;Z)→H^*(X;Z_m) fits into commutative diagrams with Bocksteins (e.g., β = ρ β).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation property of the Bockstein
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from lifting cocycles to larger coefficient groups and using the cup product on cochains. Use this product rule repeatedly to compute Bocksteins of products and thereby deduce cup product structure with integral coefficients from mod-p data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of Bockstein in K(Z_m,1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X = K(Z_m,1) (e.g., RP^∞ when m=2), H^n(X; Z_m) ≈ Z_m for all n, and β: H^n(X;Z_m) → H^{n+1}(X;Z_m) is an isomorphism for n odd and zero for n even (for the example discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surjectivity properties of reduction maps and exactness to determine whether β is zero or an iso in particular degrees; this yields periodic structure useful for computations (e.g., generators, relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bockstein squares to zero and Bockstein cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: β^2 = 0, so (H^*(X; Z_p), β) is a chain complex and one defines Bockstein cohomology BH^n(X; Z_p) = Ker β / Im β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat β as a boundary operator to form BH groups; these capture pieces of integral cohomology information that survive reduction to Z_p and are central to recovering Z-coefficient structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3E.3: rules determining BH from H^*(X; Z)
rubrics_metrics.description: If H^n(X; Z) is finitely generated for all n, then with p prime: (a) each Z summand of H^n(X; Z) contributes a Z_p summand to BH^n(X; Z_p); (b) each Z_{p^k} summand with k>1 contributes Z_p summands to both BH^{n-1}(X; Z_p) and BH^n(X; Z_p); (c) a Z_p summand of H^n(X; Z) gives Z_p summands of H^{n-1}(X; Z_p) and H^n(X; Z_p) with β an isomorphism between them, hence contributes nothing to BH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose integral cohomology into cyclic summands and apply these rules to read off Bockstein cohomology; the proof uses minimal chain complexes and dualization, and indicates how p-torsion of different exponents shows up in BH.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3E.4: characterization via BH dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: H^*(X; Z) contains no elements of order p^2 iff dim_{Z_p} BH^n(X; Z_p) equals rank H^n(X; Z) for all n. In that case ρ: H^*(X; Z)→H^*(X; Z_p) is injective on p-torsion and the image of the p-torsion under ρ equals Im β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the equality of BH dimensions and ranks as a diagnostic for absence of p^2-torsion; if satisfied, integral p-torsion injects into mod-p cohomology and is exactly the image of the Bockstein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Bocksteins to compute cup products in lens spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For infinite-dimensional lens space L = S^∞/Z_m, even-dimensional cohomology with Z_m coefficients maps isomorphically to CP^∞ even-degree cohomology; if y ∈ H^2(L; Z_m) and x ∈ H^1(L; Z_m) with β(x)=y, then β(x y^k) = y^{k+1}. For odd m, H^*(L; Z_m) ≈ Z_m[x] ⊗ Z_m[y] with x^2 = 0; for even m, x^2 is the unique order-2 element in H^2(L; Z_m). Finite lens spaces are obtained by truncating via y^{n+1}=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute cup products by tracking generators and Bockstein images; the derivation property and identification of generators let you determine the entire multiplicative structure modulo relations and truncation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product computations and Bockstein diagrams (RP^∞ × RP^∞ example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In H^*(RP^∞ × RP^∞; Z_2) ≈ Z_2[x,y], Bocksteins satisfy β(x^{2k-1}) = x^{2k}, β(x^{2k})=0; applying product formula gives a grid of Ker/Im patterns. For RP^∞×RP^∞ one finds Ker β = Im β except in degree 0, Im β is the subring Z_2[x^2,y^2] plus multiples of x^2 y + x y^2, and integral cohomology ring is H^*(RP^∞×RP^∞; Z) ≈ Z[λ, μ, ν]/(2λ,2μ,2ν, ν^2 + λ^2 μ + λ μ^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent monomials graphically to visualize Bockstein arrows; use Ker/Im patterns to reconstruct integral ring including 2-torsion and relations that arise from squaring patterns in mod-2 cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: cohomology rings of factors do not determine product ring
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist finite CW complexes X1 and X2 with isomorphic rings H^*(X1; Z) ≈ H^*(X2; Z) but a space Y such that H^*(X1×Y; Z) and H^*(X2×Y; Z) are isomorphic only as groups, not as rings. This can occur only if all three factors have torsion in Z-cohomology; Bockstein computations on products detect differences in cup products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When torsion is present, compute Bocksteins in the factors and use product formula for β (and for cross products) to see how torsion classes interact under cup/cross products to alter multiplicative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute integral cohomology of SO(n) via Bocksteins
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the pattern of Bocksteins in H^*(SO(n); Z_2) together with Proposition 3E.3 and Corollary 3E.4 to deduce H^*(SO(n); Z) (modulo odd torsion) and sometimes fully (when odd torsion absent). Examples: explicit presentations for H^*(SO(5); Z) and H^*(SO(7); Z) are given, with generators and relations (including 2-torsion relations and nontrivial squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draw the diagram of mod-2 cohomology generators and nontrivial Bockstein arrows; read off Im β and BH to reconstruct integral groups and then analyze multiplicative relations (sometimes resulting in complicated presentations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct limits for homology under unions of subcomplexes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is the union of an increasing sequence of subcomplexes X_0 ⊂ X_1 ⊂ ···, then H_n(X; G) ≅ lim_{→} H_n(X_i; G) for ordinary homology (and more generally for any homology theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mapping telescope models and Proposition 3.33 / Theorem 3F.8 to justify passing to direct limits for homology; apply to examples like telescopes of degree-p maps where H_n(T) ≅ Z[1/p].

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse limits and cohomology with field coefficients (Proposition 3F.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X = ⋃ X_i and G is Q or Z_p (a field), then the natural map λ: H^n(X; G) → lim_{←} H^n(X_i; G) is an isomorphism for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses Hom(lim_{→} H_n(X_i; G), G) ≅ lim_{←} Hom(H_n(X_i; G), G) for fields. When coefficients are fields, cohomology commutes with this inverse limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3F.8: lim^1 exact sequence for cohomology theories
rubrics_metrics.description: For a CW complex X = ⋃ X_i and any (reduced or unreduced) cohomology theory h^*, there is an exact sequence 0 → lim^1 h^{n-1}(X_i) → h^n(X) → lim_{←} h^n(X_i) → 0. For homology theories, the natural maps lim_{→} h_n(X_i) → h_n(X) are isomorphisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect a possible nontrivial lim^1 obstruction when reconstructing cohomology from inverse systems of subcomplexes; check vanishing criteria (e.g., surjective transition maps give lim^1=0) and use mapping-telescope/Mayer–Vietoris arguments in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic description and properties of lim and lim^1
rubrics_metrics.description: For an inverse sequence ··· → G_2 → G_1 → G_0, lim_{←} G_i is the subgroup of ∏ G_i of compatible sequences; lim^1 G_i is the cokernel of δ: ∏ G_i → ∏ G_i where δ(···, g_i, ···) = (···, g_i − α_{i+1}(g_{i+1}), ···). lim^1 vanishes if all transition maps are surjective (or if all are isomorphisms). Deleting finitely many initial terms doesn't change lim or lim^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these algebraic characterizations to compute examples (e.g., p-adic integers Z_p as lim of Z/p^i, lim^1 may be nonzero in other sequences such as Z_p→Z_p/Z examples). Recognize that lim^1 can produce large, sometimes uncountable, groups in cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping telescope examples illustrating limit phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping telescope of degree-p maps S^n→S^n has H_n(T) ≅ Z[1/p] (direct limit behavior) but H^{n+1}(T; Z) ≅ Z_p/Z (cohomology concentrates one degree higher), showing cohomology may behave counterintuitively due to lim^1 terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing telescopes or unions with noncompact behavior, compute both homology (direct limits) and cohomology (use Theorem 3F.8 and check lim^1). The examples warn that cohomology does not always pass to limits as straightforwardly as homology.
